title: Page Cache Pressure and Reclaim Activity
exclusions: This host-level signal does not identify the process, cgroup, NUMA node, or allocation that caused pressure; detect an OOM kill; or prove that every page counted by aggregate `pgscan_*` and `pgsteal_*` was file-backed. `nr_file_pages` and `workingset_refault_file` provide page-cache context, while PSI confirms workload impact. The search intentionally omits hosts with missing PSI, missing counters, counter resets, duplicate samples, or sample gaps over 180 seconds; monitor those conditions separately as telemetry failures. Windows, per-cgroup pressure, planned stress tests, and hosts with a current, approved entry in `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv` are outside the alert scope.
evidence: For each firing, retain the `linux_page_cache_pressure_and_reclaim_activity` saved-search definition and result row containing `host`, `_time`, five-sample PSI and reclaim rates, file-cache size, refault rate, reclaim efficiency, and sample counts. Preserve the matching raw `linux:vmreclaim` events, the deployed `TA-linux-vmreclaim` configuration bundle, and the ticket-backed exception lookup revision for the same time range; these artifacts show what the search observed without asserting a root cause.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Index six one-minute `linux:vmreclaim` events for one test host and one unchanged `boot_id`, with `page_size_bytes=4096`. Across each adjacent pair, increase the combined `pgscan_direct` plus `pgscan_kswapd` counters by at least 15,360 pages (1 MiB/s for 60 seconds), increase `pgscan_direct`, keep all counters monotonic, and set `psi_memory_some_avg60=6.00`. Leave the host absent from `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv`. Run the saved search over the fixture and confirm one row after five valid deltas, with `pressure_samples>=3`, positive direct-reclaim rate, and correctly calculated MiB/s values.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run three independent negative fixtures and confirm zero rows: (1) use the same reclaim-counter increments but keep `psi_memory_some_avg60=1.00`; (2) set PSI above 5 percent but leave all scan counters flat; and (3) reset counters while changing `boot_id`, proving that the search never differences across a reboot. Then add the positive fixture host to `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv` with a future UTC `valid_until` value and confirm suppression; an expired exception must not suppress it.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=linux:vmreclaim`, one event per host every 60 seconds from a Universal Forwarder scripted input. Each event carries cumulative `/proc/vmstat` counters (`pgscan_direct`, `pgscan_kswapd`, `pgsteal_direct`, `pgsteal_kswapd`, `workingset_refault_file`), page-count gauges (`nr_file_pages`, `nr_active_file`, `nr_inactive_file`), `page_size_bytes`, `boot_id`, `sample_epoch`, and `some`/`full` averages and totals parsed from `/proc/pressure/memory`.
app: Customer-managed `TA-linux-vmreclaim` app deployed to Splunk Universal Forwarders. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) may coexist for other host telemetry, but its standard `vmstat.sh` output is not assumed to contain the raw `/proc/vmstat` counters and PSI fields required here.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux:vmreclaim earliest=-15m@m latest=@m
| eval _time=tonumber(sample_epoch), page_size_bytes=tonumber(page_size_bytes), pgscan_direct=tonumber(pgscan_direct), pgscan_kswapd=tonumber(pgscan_kswapd), pgsteal_direct=tonumber(pgsteal_direct), pgsteal_kswapd=tonumber(pgsteal_kswapd), nr_file_pages=tonumber(nr_file_pages), nr_active_file=tonumber(nr_active_file), nr_inactive_file=tonumber(nr_inactive_file), workingset_refault_file=tonumber(workingset_refault_file), psi_memory_some_avg60=tonumber(psi_memory_some_avg60), psi_memory_full_avg60=tonumber(psi_memory_full_avg60)
| where isnotnull(_time) AND isnotnull(boot_id) AND page_size_bytes>0 AND isnotnull(pgscan_direct) AND isnotnull(pgscan_kswapd) AND isnotnull(pgsteal_direct) AND isnotnull(pgsteal_kswapd) AND isnotnull(nr_file_pages) AND isnotnull(workingset_refault_file) AND isnotnull(psi_memory_some_avg60) AND isnotnull(psi_memory_full_avg60)
| sort 0 host boot_id _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 global=f last(_time) AS prev_time last(pgscan_direct) AS prev_pgscan_direct last(pgscan_kswapd) AS prev_pgscan_kswapd last(pgsteal_direct) AS prev_pgsteal_direct last(pgsteal_kswapd) AS prev_pgsteal_kswapd last(workingset_refault_file) AS prev_workingset_refault_file BY host boot_id
| eval elapsed_sec=_time-prev_time
| where elapsed_sec>=30 AND elapsed_sec<=180 AND pgscan_direct>=prev_pgscan_direct AND pgscan_kswapd>=prev_pgscan_kswapd AND pgsteal_direct>=prev_pgsteal_direct AND pgsteal_kswapd>=prev_pgsteal_kswapd AND workingset_refault_file>=prev_workingset_refault_file
| eval scan_pages_delta=(pgscan_direct-prev_pgscan_direct)+(pgscan_kswapd-prev_pgscan_kswapd), direct_scan_pages_delta=pgscan_direct-prev_pgscan_direct, reclaimed_pages_delta=(pgsteal_direct-prev_pgsteal_direct)+(pgsteal_kswapd-prev_pgsteal_kswapd), file_refault_delta=workingset_refault_file-prev_workingset_refault_file
| eval scan_mib_per_sec=round((scan_pages_delta*page_size_bytes)/(elapsed_sec*1048576),3), direct_scan_mib_per_sec=round((direct_scan_pages_delta*page_size_bytes)/(elapsed_sec*1048576),3), reclaimed_mib_per_sec=round((reclaimed_pages_delta*page_size_bytes)/(elapsed_sec*1048576),3), file_refaults_per_sec=round(file_refault_delta/elapsed_sec,3), reclaim_efficiency_pct=if(scan_pages_delta>0,round(100*reclaimed_pages_delta/scan_pages_delta,2),null()), file_cache_mib=round((nr_file_pages*page_size_bytes)/1048576,1)
| bin _time span=1m
| stats avg(scan_mib_per_sec) AS scan_mib_per_sec avg(direct_scan_mib_per_sec) AS direct_scan_mib_per_sec avg(reclaimed_mib_per_sec) AS reclaimed_mib_per_sec avg(file_refaults_per_sec) AS file_refaults_per_sec avg(reclaim_efficiency_pct) AS reclaim_efficiency_pct latest(file_cache_mib) AS file_cache_mib max(psi_memory_some_avg60) AS psi_memory_some_avg60 max(psi_memory_full_avg60) AS psi_memory_full_avg60 count AS samples_in_minute BY host _time
| eval pressure_sample=if(psi_memory_some_avg60>=5 AND scan_mib_per_sec>=1 AND (direct_scan_mib_per_sec>0 OR file_refaults_per_sec>0),1,0)
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats window=5 current=t global=f count AS window_samples sum(pressure_sample) AS pressure_samples avg(scan_mib_per_sec) AS scan_mib_per_sec_5sample avg(direct_scan_mib_per_sec) AS direct_scan_mib_per_sec_5sample avg(reclaimed_mib_per_sec) AS reclaimed_mib_per_sec_5sample avg(file_refaults_per_sec) AS file_refaults_per_sec_5sample avg(reclaim_efficiency_pct) AS reclaim_efficiency_pct_5sample avg(psi_memory_some_avg60) AS psi_memory_some_avg60_5sample max(psi_memory_full_avg60) AS psi_memory_full_avg60_peak BY host
| where window_samples=5 AND pressure_samples>=3
| stats latest(_time) AS _time latest(pressure_samples) AS pressure_samples latest(scan_mib_per_sec_5sample) AS scan_mib_per_sec_5sample latest(direct_scan_mib_per_sec_5sample) AS direct_scan_mib_per_sec_5sample latest(reclaimed_mib_per_sec_5sample) AS reclaimed_mib_per_sec_5sample latest(file_refaults_per_sec_5sample) AS file_refaults_per_sec_5sample latest(reclaim_efficiency_pct_5sample) AS reclaim_efficiency_pct_5sample latest(psi_memory_some_avg60_5sample) AS psi_memory_some_avg60_5sample latest(psi_memory_full_avg60_peak) AS psi_memory_full_avg60_peak latest(file_cache_mib) AS file_cache_mib BY host
| lookup linux_capacity_exceptions.csv host OUTPUT valid_until reason AS exception_reason
| eval valid_until_epoch=if(isnum(valid_until),tonumber(valid_until),strptime(valid_until,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"))
| where isnull(valid_until_epoch) OR valid_until_epoch<now()
| table _time host pressure_samples scan_mib_per_sec_5sample direct_scan_mib_per_sec_5sample reclaimed_mib_per_sec_5sample reclaim_efficiency_pct_5sample file_refaults_per_sec_5sample file_cache_mib psi_memory_some_avg60_5sample psi_memory_full_avg60_peak
description: Detects sustained host memory pressure when Linux is actively scanning reclaimable pages and workload stalls are measurable. It converts cumulative `/proc/vmstat` counters to reboot-safe MiB/s rates using the host page size, adds page-cache size and file-refault context, and requires corroborating memory PSI before returning an alert.
value: Direct reclaim stalls allocating tasks, while repeated eviction and refault of useful file data can turn memory contention into application latency and storage I/O. Corroborating reclaim with measured stalls shortens triage by helping platform teams distinguish active pressure from a merely small free-memory value and prioritize workload, cache, swap, or capacity investigation before an OOM event.
implementation: Deploy a 60-second scripted input that emits raw, cumulative `/proc/vmstat` values together with `/proc/pressure/memory`, boot identity, sample time, and base page size. Save the SPL over a 15-minute range; it derives rates in search time, rejects resets and stale intervals, and alerts only when at least three of five samples exceed the documented advisory PSI and scan-rate guardrails.
visualization: Four aligned host panels: memory PSI `some`/`full` percentages over 24 hours; total and direct scan MiB/s beside reclaimed MiB/s; reclaim-efficiency percentage; and file-cache MiB with file refaults/s. The alert table should retain every final SPL column and drill down to the raw six-event sequence.

knownFalsePositives:
The search reports a real combination of reclaim work and measured stalls; a firing can still be expected or non-actionable.

1. **Approved `stress-ng` memory-pressure test** — A bounded lab or pre-production test can intentionally raise `pgscan_direct`, `pgscan_kswapd`, and memory PSI. Match the host, test command, owner, ticket, and UTC start/end times; retain the result as test evidence and suppress only notification delivery during that approved interval.

2. **Short-lived Spark, database, or analytics batch** — A scheduled memory-intensive job can produce direct reclaim and file refaults while still meeting its service objective. Correlate the exact five-sample window with the named job run, p95/p99 latency, swap activity, and completion status; recurring production pressure outside the approved run remains actionable.

3. **Backup, antivirus, or filesystem scan** — Veeam agents, `clamd`, or a deployment-owned scanner can read a large working set and intentionally churn `nr_file_pages` and `workingset_refault_file`. Confirm the process, scan policy, storage I/O, and maintenance record before treating the alert as expected; do not create a permanent host exclusion for a recurring scan.

4. **Hypervisor ballooning or VM-density change** — VMware ballooning, KVM virtio-balloon activity, or a host consolidation can reduce guest memory and cause genuine reclaim stalls. Compare the alert minute with guest balloon telemetry, hypervisor changes, and workload latency; route an approved density test to the virtualization owner rather than hiding subsequent unexplained pressure.

5. **Cache warm-up after reboot or deployment** — Restarting PostgreSQL, an application server, or a large service can cause temporary eviction and refault while its working set is rebuilt. Require matching boot ID or deployment evidence and confirm that PSI and refault rates decay within the owner-approved warm-up window before closing the finding.

6. **Efficient background reclaim on a large host** — A high `reclaim_efficiency_pct` is not itself harmful; it means scans found reclaimable pages. Distinguish it with the required PSI and direct-scan/refault signals plus service latency. There is no portable efficiency cutoff, so tune by hardware and workload class rather than filtering on the ratio alone.

Approved suppression uses the existing `lookup linux_capacity_exceptions.csv host OUTPUT valid_until exception_reason` followed by the expiry filter `where isnull(valid_until_epoch) OR valid_until_epoch<now()`. Treat every row as a time-bound exception: key it to the exact host, require epoch seconds or UTC `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` in `valid_until`, and record owner, ticket, and reason in the governed change record. Reject wildcards, missing expiry, and permanent entries; preserve raw samples and base search results.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux memory-performance monitoring; no security technique asserted)
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites

Use a Linux host whose procfs exposes all required aggregate reclaim counters and `/proc/pressure/memory`. PSI availability depends on the kernel configuration and runtime environment; containers can hide the host pressure files even when the host kernel supports PSI. Run `test -r /proc/vmstat -a -r /proc/pressure/memory -a -r /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` as the Universal Forwarder service account. Confirm the exact keys with `awk '$1 ~ /^(pgscan_(direct|kswapd)|pgsteal_(direct|kswapd)|nr_(file_pages|active_file|inactive_file)|workingset_refault_file)$/ {print}' /proc/vmstat`. Do not substitute `vmstat` command columns `si` and `so`: those are swap-in and swap-out rates, not page-scan or page-steal counters.

Deploy a customer-managed app named `TA-linux-vmreclaim`; no premium Splunk app or CIM acceleration is required. The forwarder account needs read access to the three procfs files and execute access to the script, but it does not need root. Search users need access to `index=os`, the saved search, and the exception lookup. Establish `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv` with header `host,valid_until,reason`; use an empty file with that header when no exceptions exist. Record the host's base page size rather than assuming 4 KiB, because `/proc/vmstat` scan, steal, cache, and refault values are page counts and Linux page size is architecture-specific.

Step 1 — Configure a raw-counter scripted input

Create `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-vmreclaim/bin/collect_vmreclaim.sh` from `scriptExample`, set mode 0755, and keep Unix line endings. The collector deliberately emits cumulative counters, not deltas. Search-time differencing can then use `_time`, `boot_id`, and explicit reset checks; a collector-side state file would otherwise introduce races, permission failures, and silent spikes after restart. One invocation produces one space-delimited key-value event per host, approximately one kilobyte per minute.

Create `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-vmreclaim/local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://./bin/collect_vmreclaim.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
source = linux_vmreclaim
sourcetype = linux:vmreclaim
```

Create `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA-linux-vmreclaim/local/props.conf`:

```ini
[linux:vmreclaim]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
KV_MODE = auto
```

Deploy the app through the deployment server and restart or reload the forwarder as required by local change policy. The optional Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux may continue collecting its normal host metrics; do not relabel its built-in `vmstat.sh` events as `linux:vmreclaim`, because this search requires raw kernel counters, PSI lanes, page size, sample epoch, and boot identity in one event.

Step 2 — Verify units, continuity, and field extraction

Run `index=os sourcetype=linux:vmreclaim earliest=-10m | table _time host sample_epoch boot_id page_size_bytes pgscan_direct pgscan_kswapd pgsteal_direct pgsteal_kswapd nr_file_pages workingset_refault_file psi_memory_some_avg60 psi_memory_full_avg60`. Expect one row per host per minute. `sample_epoch` is seconds since the Unix epoch; PSI `avg10`, `avg60`, and `avg300` are percentages; PSI `total` is cumulative microseconds; the vmstat counters and gauges are pages; and the SPL's rate fields are MiB/s using 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes. There is no vendor UI for this procfs feed: compare with the live kernel interface by taking a near-simultaneous local read of `/proc/vmstat`, `/proc/pressure/memory`, `getconf PAGESIZE`, and the boot ID. Exact cumulative values should match or differ only by activity during collection and forwarding.

Check continuity with `index=os sourcetype=linux:vmreclaim earliest=-24h | eval sample_epoch=tonumber(sample_epoch) | sort 0 host sample_epoch | streamstats current=f window=1 last(sample_epoch) AS previous BY host | eval gap=sample_epoch-previous | where gap>180`. Any result is a data-quality incident for this use case. Duplicate writers are also invalid: if two deployment apps emit the sourcetype for one host, zero-second or interleaved deltas distort rates. Keep one writer per host.

Step 3 — Create and understand the saved search

Save the primary SPL exactly as `linux_page_cache_pressure_and_reclaim_activity`, schedule it every five minutes, and retain `earliest=-15m@m latest=@m`. The closed latest boundary avoids evaluating a partially indexed minute. Trigger once per returned host and throttle that host for fifteen minutes; do not use a real-time search. A fifteen-minute scan supplies enough history for six or more raw events while the final decision uses five valid one-minute rate samples.

The first `eval` converts extracted strings to numbers and replaces index time with collector `sample_epoch`. The null guard prevents malformed events from becoming zeroes. Sorting by host, boot ID, and sample time is mandatory before `streamstats`; `current=f window=1` attaches the immediately preceding sample from the same boot. The 30-to-180-second interval guard tolerates modest scheduling jitter but rejects duplicates and long gaps. Monotonic checks reject resets or malformed negative deltas.

The next stages sum direct and background scan counters and convert pages to MiB/s with the reported page size. `pgscan_*` represents pages examined by reclaim and `pgsteal_*` pages reclaimed. Their ratio is displayed as reclaim efficiency: a larger ratio means scans found more reclaimable pages, so the former rule `pgsteal/pgscan > 0.7` must not be described as heavy reclaim or as a failure threshold. `nr_file_pages` supplies the current file-cache gauge, and `workingset_refault_file` shows file-backed pages needed again after eviction. Neither makes the aggregate scan counters file-only, which is why the exclusions retain that limitation.

The default candidate condition requires PSI memory `some avg60` of at least 5 percent, aggregate scanning of at least 1 MiB/s, and either direct scanning or file refaults, in at least three of five samples. These values are operational starting guardrails, not Linux-kernel limits or vendor promises. Baseline them by hardware and workload class for at least two normal weeks, then raise or lower them against observed application latency and throughput. Preserve PSI corroboration when tuning so a large server's harmless background scan volume does not page an operator merely because it is large. `full avg60` is retained for urgency context: the kernel defines `full` as all non-idle tasks stalled simultaneously, but this use case does not invent a universal severity boundary for it.

Step 4 — Validate positive, negative, and reset behavior

For the positive control, load the six-event fixture described in `controlTest` into a non-production test index, temporarily replace `index=os` with that index, and keep the same host and boot ID. With 4,096-byte pages, 15,360 scanned pages over 60 seconds equals exactly 1 MiB/s. Confirm the first raw event produces no delta, the next five produce valid rates, and at least three set `pressure_sample=1`. Check the calculated scan and steal rates by hand from two adjacent events.

For negative controls, independently lower PSI, flatten scan counters, change boot ID while resetting counters, and introduce a gap over 180 seconds. Each must return no alert. Test lookup behavior with one future and one expired `valid_until`; malformed dates do not suppress and should be corrected by lookup governance. Do not run `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` on production to test this alert. In an isolated lab, an approved memory-pressure tool can create reclaim, but stop it under a documented safety limit and compare the Splunk row with `vmstat 1`, the two procfs files, workload latency, and storage I/O.

Step 5 — Operationalize and troubleshoot

Place PSI above reclaim throughput on the dashboard so responders see impact before mechanism. Show direct scan separately from kswapd activity, overlay file refaults on file-cache size, and retain reclaim efficiency as diagnostic context rather than a red/green KPI. When the alert fires, first confirm ingestion continuity and an unchanged boot ID; then correlate the same window with swap rates, major faults, disk latency, deployment or batch schedules, cgroup pressure, and application SLOs. Possible responses include moving or limiting a noisy workload, correcting an undersized cgroup or VM, reviewing swap and kernel watermark policy with a Linux specialist, or adding memory. Never change `swappiness`, watermarks, or drop caches from the alert action.

No events with `ExecProcessor` errors usually means the script is not executable, the forwarder account cannot read a procfs path, or the runtime hides PSI. Run the script as the forwarder account and inspect stderr in `_internal`. Events with missing fields indicate a kernel field-name mismatch or broken key-value output; fail the collector and update the compatibility contract rather than coalescing absent counters to zero. Rates that spike after reboot indicate `boot_id` was omitted or not partitioned. Rates approximately 4,096 times too large indicate page counts were treated as bytes; rates off by sixty indicate a per-minute delta was labeled per second. Empty alerts despite visible pressure commonly mean fewer than six raw events, gaps above 180 seconds, no direct scan or refault corroboration, or an active exception. Excess alerts during legitimate batch windows require workload-specific baselining and ticketed, expiring exceptions—not removal of PSI or reset guards.
grandmaExplanation: We watch whether a server is repeatedly clearing useful stored data from memory while programs are being made to wait. That helps the team act before the slowdown grows into a larger outage.
